extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and students of astronomy (19th-century popular scientific audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A popular-science textbook chapter describing the physical structure, observable properties, orbital elements, and historical study of comets, intended to explain how comets are observed, identified, and understood. Emphasizes observational criteria, orbital calculation, and historical examples (Halley, 1680, 1770, 1811, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comet parts: nucleus, envelope (coma), and tail
rubrics_metrics.description: A comet, when perfectly formed, consists of three parts, the nucleus, the envelope, and the tail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the nucleus is a bright central point (sometimes absent or very small), the envelope or 'coma' is a dense nebulous covering (called 'coma' from Latin for hair), and the tail is an expansion/prolongation of the coma. Notes a gradation from purely gaseous comets to those with well-defined nuclei, that some comets show stars through the densest part, and gives examples of relative sizes (nucleus sometimes measurable by telescope; some nuclei as small as ~25 miles, others hundreds of miles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify comet identity by orbital path, not appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: The appearances of the same comet at different returns are so various that one must judge identity by its path through the heavens (as traced among the stars), not by color, magnitude, or shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that physical aspect varies greatly between returns (examples: Halley's varying tail length and brightness across centuries) and that historical accounts of appearance are often exaggerated or inconsistent; accurate positional/path data are required to assert identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orbital elements as sufficient data to determine path
rubrics_metrics.description: The particulars called the 'elements' of a comet (nodes, inclination, perihelion distance, longitude of perihelion, etc.) afford sufficient data for determining a comet's path.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists the elements Halley calculated: points where the comet crosses the ecliptic (nodes), inclination of the orbit to the ecliptic, perihelion distance (nearest approach to the sun), longitude of the perihelion, and the course (prograde/retrograde). Shows Halley's tabular comparison of these elements across epochs as the method to identify recurring comets and predict returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow for planetary perturbations when comparing intervals/paths
rubrics_metrics.description: Intervals between successive returns and small differences in orbital inclination/element values may be explained by the disturbing action of planets (notably Jupiter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Halley's reasoning: cometary periods and orbital directions vary because gravitational perturbations by planets alter comet velocities and orbital elements (analogy to planetary perturbations like Jupiter's effect on Saturn). Therefore, small inequalities in observed return intervals or element values do not disprove identity of a periodic comet; calculations of perturbations must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tail direction: tails extend away from the sun
rubrics_metrics.description: The tails of comets extend in a direct line from the sun, although more or less curved, and are usually convex on the side next to the direction in which they are moving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that tails are turned from the sun (Pierre Appian's observation confirmed by later work), often increase as the comet approaches the sun, may be divided into portions (central less bright than marginal), can show expansions on the sunward side, and may present multiple tails (example: comet of 1744 with six tails). Tail curvature may result from velocity differences along the tail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brightness and apparent magnitude depend on geometry and real change
rubrics_metrics.description: Magnitude and brightness vary greatly between comets and between returns; visibility depends on distance from sun, position of Earth relative to the comet, and real changes in the comet's emitted/reflected light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical records report comets visible in daytime and tails extending many degrees, but such accounts may be exaggerated. Apparent size and brightness depend on observer location and viewing angle; the same comet shows different aspects at different returns (Halley's comet examples: 1305, 1456, 1682, 1759, 1835). Observers should consider geometric factors and real physical changes when interpreting brightness reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comets shine predominantly by reflected sunlight (polarization evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comets shine by reflecting the light of the sun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that polarization experiments (M. Arago on the comet of 1819) indicate reflected light, though some astronomers hypothesized self-luminous matter. The thin vapor-like nature of cometary material means relatively little light is required for visibility when illuminated through a large volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cometary mass is very small; inferable from gravitational effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of matter in comets is exceedingly small; their tails consist of extremely tenuous matter and comets may pass near planets without appreciably disturbing planetary motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides empirical inference: example of the 1770 comet that came near Jupiter's satellites and near Earth but produced no sensible planetary perturbation; La Place's estimate that the comet's mass could not exceed 1/5000 of Earth's mass (and likely much less). Also notes that comets themselves are strongly disturbed by planetary gravity, consistent with having little mass relative to planets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orbital shape and eccentricity determine observability and velocity variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cometary orbits are often highly eccentric, so comets are visible only when near the sun and traverse their orbits at very different speeds in different parts: extremely slow at aphelion and extremely fast at perihelion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: comet of 1680 came very near the sun (one-sixth of sun's diameter from surface) and had perihelion velocity exceeding a million miles an hour; long orbital periods (hundreds to thousands of years) mean most of the orbit is unobservable. This informs when and how long comets are available for observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical-method criterion: compare recorded elements across epochs to detect periodic comets
rubrics_metrics.description: Halley's method: examine recorded comets with sufficiently precise observations, compute their orbital elements, and compare these elements to identify recurrences and predict future returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance from the text: only records with sufficiently accurate positional/element data (post-1300 examples) are usable; Halley examined 24 comets with adequate observations, compared inclinations, nodes, perihelion longitudes and distances, and used concordance (allowing for perturbations) to assert periodicity (e.g., the 1531, 1607, 1682 returns as Halley's comet, period ≈ 75.5 years).
